svg.text: Children are dosed by weight, so the weight must be right
Every paediatric drug error starts somewhere in this chain
The four steps, and what goes wrong at each
1. Weigh the child today — a weight from last admission is the wrong child’s weight
2. Multiply dose per kilogram by the weight — and check it against the maximum
3. Convert milligrams to millilitres using the strength on this bottle, not the usual one
4. Have a second nurse repeat the calculation independently, not simply agree with yours
Worked example
Paracetamol 15 mg/kg for a child of 12 kg
15 × 12 = 180 mg per dose
Bottle reads 120 mg in 5 mL
More milligrams than the bottle strength, so more than 5 mL
The answers that should stop you
A volume larger than the child could swallow
A dose bigger than an adult would receive
A tenfold difference from what you expected
A decimal point you had to think about
A wrong decimal is a tenfold error, not a small one
Why children are harmed more than adults by the same mistake
A small child has little reserve, so an overdose is a larger multiple of what the body can handle
The doses are small, so a misplaced decimal point produces a tenfold or hundredfold error
A young child cannot say “this is not my usual medicine” — the last safety net is missing
